questions.text: Let [latex] G [/latex] be a directed graph and [latex] T [/latex] a depth first search (DFS) spanning tree in [latex] G [/latex] that is rooted at a vertex [latex] v [/latex]. Suppose [latex] T [/latex] is also a breadth first search (BFS) tree in [latex] G [/latex], rooted at [latex] v [/latex]. Which of the following statements is/are TRUE for every such graph [latex] G [/latex] and tree [latex] T [/latex] ?
questions.solution:
In a BFS tree, every edge [latex]u\rightarrow w[/latex] of G satisfies [latex]level(w)\le level(u)+1[/latex].

A forward edge goes from [latex]u[/latex] to a non-child descendant [latex]w[/latex], so [latex]level(w)\ge level(u)+2[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] this contradicts BFS. Hence there are no forward edges [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.

The others can fail:
- Back edge: G = {v[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]a, a[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]v}. Tree {v[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]a} is both DFS and BFS tree; a[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]v is a back edge.
- Cross edge: G = {v[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]a, v[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]b, b[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]a}. DFS visits a then b; b[latex]\rightarrow[/latex]a is a cross edge, and the tree is also the BFS tree.
- So G can also have edges outside T.

Answer: There are no forward-edges in G with respect to T

options: There are no back-edges in [latex] G [/latex] with respect to the tree [latex] T [/latex]
There are no cross-edges in [latex] G [/latex] with respect to the tree [latex] T [/latex]
There are no forward-edges in [latex] G [/latex] with respect to the tree [latex] T [/latex]
The only edges in [latex] G [/latex] are the edges in [latex] T [/latex]

questions.text: Let [latex]A [/latex] and [latex]B [/latex] be non-empty finite sets such that there exist one-to-one and onto functions (i) from [latex]A [/latex] to [latex]B [/latex] and (ii) from [latex]A \times A [/latex] to [latex]A \cup B [/latex]. The number of possible values of [latex]|A| [/latex] is ___
questions.solution:
Bijection [latex]A\to B[/latex] [latex]\Rightarrow[/latex] [latex]|A|=|B|=n[/latex].
Bijection [latex]A\times A\to A\cup B[/latex] [latex]\Rightarrow[/latex] [latex]n^2=|A\cup B|[/latex].

But [latex]n\le|A\cup B|\le 2n[/latex], so [latex]n\le n^2\le 2n[/latex] [latex]\Rightarrow[/latex] [latex]n\le2[/latex].

- [latex]n=1[/latex]: [latex]A=B[/latex], [latex]|A\cup B|=1=1^2[/latex] True
- [latex]n=2[/latex]: take A and B disjoint, [latex]|A\cup B|=4=2^2[/latex] True

So [latex]|A|\in\{1,2\}[/latex].

Answer: 2

questions.text: Let [latex]A [/latex] and [latex]B [/latex] be two events in a probability space with [latex]P(A)=0.3, P(B)=0.5 [/latex], and [latex]P(A \cap B)=0.1 [/latex]. Which of the following statements is/are TRUE?
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- Independence: [latex]P(A)P(B)=0.15\ne0.1[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.
- [latex]P(A\cup B)=0.3+0.5-0.1=0.7[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- [latex]P(A\cap B^c)=P(A)-P(A\cap B)=0.3-0.1=0.2[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- [latex]P(A^c\cap B^c)=1-P(A\cup B)=0.3\ne0.4[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.

Answer: [latex]P(A\cup B)=0.7[/latex] and [latex]P(A\cap B^c)=0.2[/latex]

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow
options: The two events [latex]A [/latex] and [latex]B [/latex] are independent
[latex]P\left(A \cap B^c\right)=0.2 [/latex], where [latex]B^c [/latex] is the complement of the event [latex]B [/latex]
[latex]P\left(A^c \cap B^c\right)=0.4 [/latex], where [latex]A^c [/latex] and [latex]B^c [/latex] are the complements of the events [latex]A [/latex] and [latex]B [/latex], respectively

questions.text: Consider a permutation sampled uniformly at random from the set of all permutations of [latex]\{1,2,3, \cdots, n\} [/latex] for some [latex]n \geq 4 [/latex]. Let [latex]X [/latex] be the event that 1 occurs before 2 in the permutation, and [latex]Y [/latex] the event that 3 occurs before 4 . Which one of the following statements is TRUE?
questions.solution:
By symmetry, 1 is before 2 in half of all permutations, so [latex]P(X)=\frac12[/latex]; similarly [latex]P(Y)=\frac12[/latex].

The relative order of {1,2} and the relative order of {3,4} involve different elements, and all 4 combinations (12/21 with 34/43) are equally likely, so [latex]P(X\cap Y)=\frac14=P(X)P(Y)[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] independent.

- Not mutually exclusive: 1 2 3 4 [latex]\ldots[/latex] satisfies both.
- Neither must occur: 2 1 4 3 [latex]\ldots[/latex] satisfies none.
- Equally likely, so X is not more likely than Y.

Answer: X and Y are independent

Event [latex]X [/latex] is more likely than event [latex]Y [/latex]

questions.text: Let [latex]f: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R} [/latex] be a function such that [latex]f(x)=\max \left\{x, x^3\right\}, x \in \mathbb{R} [/latex], where [latex]\mathbb{R} [/latex] is the set of all real numbers. The set of all points where [latex]f(x) [/latex] is NOT differentiable is
questions.solution:
Compare [latex]x[/latex] and [latex]x^3[/latex]: they are equal at [latex]x=-1,0,1[/latex]. So [latex]f(x)=x[/latex] for [latex]x\le -1[/latex], [latex]x^3[/latex] on [latex][-1,0][/latex], [latex]x[/latex] on [latex][0,1][/latex], [latex]x^3[/latex] for [latex]x\ge1[/latex].

At every switching point the two pieces have different slopes ([latex]\frac{d}{dx}x=1[/latex], [latex]\frac{d}{dx}x^3=3x^2[/latex]):
- [latex]x=-1[/latex]: slopes [latex]1[/latex] and [latex]3[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] corner
- [latex]x=0[/latex]: slopes [latex]0[/latex] and [latex]1[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] corner
- [latex]x=1[/latex]: slopes [latex]1[/latex] and [latex]3[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] corner

Everywhere else [latex]f[/latex] is a polynomial, hence differentiable.

Answer: [latex]\{-1,0,1\}[/latex]
